paragraphs: In America, Swamiji came across a famous agnostic. He was a noble, genuinely good man and a gifted public speaker. In his lectures he argued that religion was a waste of time. Why worry about other worlds at all? Life, he liked to say, is like an orange in your hand: the sensible thing is to squeeze every drop of juice out of it.

When the two met, Swamiji told him he agreed completely. He too had a fruit, and he too wanted all its juice. The only difference was the fruit they had picked. The agnostic had chosen the orange; Swamiji preferred the mango. For the agnostic, living here, eating, drinking and picking up a bit of scientific knowledge was enough. Fine, said Swamiji, but he had no right to insist that this one idea should satisfy everybody.

For Swamiji, that kind of life meant nothing. If all he could ever learn was how an apple drops to the ground or how an electric current jolts the nerves, he said, he would rather not live. He wanted to reach the very core of things. The agnostic was studying the ways life shows itself; Swamiji wanted to know life itself, what it really is, not only how it works. Knowing only the 'how' of everything, he said, was a game for children. He added a joke from one of the agnostic's own countrymen: if someone smoking a cigarette wrote a book about it, would that be the science of the cigarette?

Swamiji was not against science. He praised scientists and wished them well in their search. His objection was to the claim that science is all there is. A person who says that, he felt, never asks why life exists at all. If you study only the outer workings and cannot say what life is, your knowledge has no foundation. His closing words were generous: carry on with your study, and let me carry on with mine.
learn: Science and the search for meaning are not enemies; they answer different questions. Learn how things work, but don't stop asking what your life is for. And respect people whose 'fruit' differs from yours.
